prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- NASA's plans to fly a fifth and final space shuttle mission to service the Hubble Space Telescope have suffered another set-back. Atlantis was prepared to launch in September before an onboard computer failed, delaying the mission. Hubble managers say ground testing of a critical replacement computer that they hope to install on the orbiting telescope is taking longer than previously expected. And that means an additional flight delay. "Delivery in April to support a May launch, I think is a fair thing to say," said Hubble program manager Preston Burch. "Right now I think we have a very good chance of meeting a readiness date in that time frame." The additional delay is just the latest dip in an emotional rollercoaster ride for the Hubble team over the past few months. In late September, astronauts were mere weeks away from launching to Hubble aboard the space shuttle Atlantis, with spacewalks planned to make the telescope more powerful than ever and extend its expected lifespan an additional five years. That flight had to be postponed when the onboard computer that downlinks scientific data to the ground suddenly failed on September 27th. While that problem has been corrected using a back-up system, NASA managers have decided the computer needs to be completely replaced in order to keep a fully redundant back-up capability available. A spare computer was built prior to Hubble's launch in 1990, and has been warehoused at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland ever since. Initially, engineers had hoped that spare could be quickly tested, certified "flight ready," and shipped to the Kennedy Space Center in Florida to be packed aboard Atlantis in time for a February launch. But a closer evaluation of the spare shows more than six months of work will be needed to get it ready to fly. Among other issues, it was partially disassembled other the years so that parts could be used for other systems. It has been largely put back together, but now programming anomalies are cropping up. And once engineers get it in good working order, it will have to go a battery of environmental tests to make sure it is ready to hold up in the harsh conditions of space. But the engineers are confident that they will eventually overcome all the obstacles. "We've gotten a lot smarter about the condition of this unit over the last four weeks, said Burch. "We don't want to take any chances in bringing a box up there that isn't going to be 100% working to the absolute best that it can. So we want to take some extra time and make sure that we subject this to a very rigorous test program and we don't want to leave any stones unturned on the way to the launch pad."

(CNN) — NASA’s plan to fly a fifth and final space shuttle mission to service the Hubble Space Telescope has encountered another setback.

Atlantis had been scheduled to launch in September before an onboard computer failure forced a delay. Hubble managers now say that ground testing of a critical replacement computer they hope to install on the orbiting telescope is taking longer than previously expected, resulting in an additional postponement.

“Delivery in April to support a May launch, I think, is a fair thing to say,” said Hubble program manager Preston Burch. “Right now, I think we have a very good chance of meeting a readiness date in that time frame.”

The additional delay is only the latest dip in an emotional roller-coaster ride for the Hubble team over the past few months. In late September, astronauts were just weeks away from launching to Hubble aboard the space shuttle Atlantis, with spacewalks planned to make the telescope more powerful than ever and extend its expected lifespan by an additional five years.

That flight had to be postponed when the onboard computer that downlinks scientific data to the ground suddenly failed on September 27. Although that problem has been corrected using a backup system, NASA managers have decided the computer needs to be completely replaced in order to preserve a fully redundant backup capability.

A spare computer was built before Hubble’s launch in 1990 and has been stored at the Goddard Space Flight Center in Maryland ever since. Initially, engineers had hoped the spare could be quickly tested, certified as “flight ready,” and shipped to the Kennedy Space Center in Florida to be packed aboard Atlantis in time for a February launch.

However, a closer evaluation of the spare has shown that more than six months of work will be needed to prepare it for flight. Among other issues, it was partially disassembled over the years so that parts could be used for other systems. It has been largely reassembled, but programming anomalies are now emerging. Once engineers restore it to proper working order, it will have to undergo a battery of environmental tests to ensure it can withstand the harsh conditions of space.

Still, engineers are confident they will ultimately overcome all the obstacles.

“We’ve gotten a lot smarter about the condition of this unit over the last four weeks,” said Burch. “We don’t want to take any chances in bringing a box up there that isn’t going to be 100% working to the absolute best that it can. So we want to take some extra time and make sure that we subject this to a very rigorous test program, and we don’t want to leave any stones unturned on the way to the launch pad.”

**BREAKING NEWS: NASA Postpones Atlantis Hubble Repair Mission After Telescope Computer Failure**

**CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. —** NASA has postponed the space shuttle **Atlantis** mission to repair and upgrade the Hubble Space Telescope after a key onboard computer system aboard the observatory failed, agency officials said.

Atlantis had been scheduled to launch on a final servicing mission to Hubble, but NASA is now delaying the flight while engineers investigate the failure and prepare a backup plan. The problem involves Hubble’s **Science Instrument Command and Data Handling system**, the computer unit responsible for collecting, formatting and transmitting science data from the telescope’s instruments back to Earth.

Hubble program manager **Preston Burch** said the failure occurred in the system’s primary electronics channel, known as **Side A**, which has operated for years as part of the telescope’s data handling system.

“We’re taking the prudent course,” Burch said. “Before we send a shuttle crew to Hubble, we need to understand the failure, switch to the backup side if possible, and determine whether additional hardware should be flown on Atlantis.”

The failed computer is not part of Hubble’s basic pointing or navigation systems, meaning the telescope itself remains safe. However, without the data handling unit, Hubble cannot properly relay science observations from its instruments, effectively halting much of its scientific work.

NASA engineers are working to activate the redundant channel, **Side B**, which was built into the telescope as a backup but has not been used in regular operations. If the backup side can be brought online, Hubble may resume science operations. Still, NASA is considering adding a replacement computer unit to Atlantis’s cargo for the repair mission.

“This is exactly why Hubble was designed with redundancy,” Burch said. “But because the backup side has not been operated for a long time, we have to proceed carefully and methodically.”

The Atlantis mission is intended to be the final shuttle visit to Hubble. Astronauts are expected to install new instruments, replace aging components, repair existing equipment and extend the telescope’s life well into the next decade.

NASA officials said the delay could push the launch back by weeks or months, depending on how quickly engineers can test the backup system and prepare any replacement hardware for flight.

“We know the science community is eager to get Hubble back to full capability,” Burch said. “Our priority is to make sure the servicing mission has the best chance of success.”

The postponement is a major setback for one of NASA’s most anticipated shuttle flights, but agency officials emphasized that the delay is intended to increase the odds of preserving Hubble’s scientific future.

**Engineers Race to Ready Aging Hubble Replacement Computer Ahead of Atlantis’s Final Servicing Mission**

**GREENBELT, Maryland —** Inside a clean room at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center, the mood has swung for months between urgency, relief, dread and determination.

On a workbench sits a piece of hardware that suddenly became critical to one of the most beloved scientific instruments ever launched: the Hubble Space Telescope. It is not sleek. It is not new. In some ways, it is a time capsule — a replacement computer system built from decades-old components, now being prepared for a mission no one wants to get wrong.

The hardware is part of Hubble’s **Science Instrument Command and Data Handling system**, the electronics package that routes commands to the telescope’s science instruments and sends their data back to Earth. When a major failure struck Hubble in 2008, engineers were forced to delay the final servicing flight and scramble to prepare a spare unit for launch aboard **space shuttle Atlantis**.

For the Hubble team, the setback was devastating — and galvanizing.

“This is the kind of failure you always plan for, but you never want to see,” one engineer familiar with the preparations said at the time. “The telescope was healthy in many ways, but without that data-handling system, its science capability was in jeopardy.”

The failure meant NASA could not simply proceed with the long-planned servicing mission. Atlantis’s flight — already considered one of the most complex and emotionally charged shuttle missions — had to wait while engineers tested, refurbished and certified replacement electronics originally designed in an earlier era of spaceflight.

The pressure was immense. Hubble, launched in 1990, had already become a symbol of scientific resilience: blurred by a flawed mirror at first, rescued by shuttle astronauts, and transformed into one of the most productive observatories in history. Its images had entered the public imagination — star nurseries, dying stars, colliding galaxies, and the deep universe captured in astonishing detail.

Now, nearly two decades after launch, its future depended in part on a spare system that had been sitting on Earth for years.

At Goddard, engineers worked through exhaustive checks. Every circuit, connector and command pathway had to be evaluated. A component that functions perfectly in a lab still must survive launch vibrations, the harsh environment of orbit and the demands of a spacewalk installation 350 miles above Earth.

The emotional swings were sharp.

There was anxiety when the original failure forced the mission delay. There was frustration as carefully choreographed shuttle schedules had to be revised. There was nervous optimism as the spare unit powered up and began passing tests. And there was constant awareness that this was Hubble’s last scheduled house call.

Unlike earlier servicing flights, this mission carried a sense of finality. Atlantis would not be docking with the International Space Station; Hubble flies in a different orbit. That meant the mission carried added risk. A second shuttle, Endeavour, was placed on standby for a possible rescue mission — a stark reminder of the stakes.

For astronauts training underwater to rehearse the spacewalks, and for engineers preparing the replacement hardware on the ground, the mission became both a technical challenge and a personal one.

Many members of the Hubble team had spent large portions of their careers with the telescope. Some helped recover it after the mirror problem. Others watched it rewrite astronomy textbooks. The thought of losing Hubble prematurely — not because its optics had failed, but because its aging electronics could no longer support science operations — was difficult to accept.

The replacement computer was only one part of Atlantis’s ambitious servicing plan. Astronauts were also scheduled to install new instruments, replace gyroscopes and batteries, repair existing equipment and leave Hubble more capable than ever. But the data-handling unit became a symbol of the mission’s urgency: old technology, painstakingly revived, offering Hubble a new lease on life.

As Atlantis’s launch approached, confidence grew — but so did the tension.

Engineers knew that once the shuttle reached orbit, their work would be in the astronauts’ gloved hands. The replacement unit would have to be installed during a spacewalk, with limited time and no simple way to recover from certain mistakes. Years of preparation would come down to procedures executed in weightlessness, against the backdrop of Earth.

For NASA, the mission represented a final act of maintenance for a telescope that had repeatedly exceeded expectations. For the Hubble team, it was something more personal: a chance to keep a scientific icon alive.

The emotional rollercoaster — the shock of failure, the urgency of recovery, the painstaking revival of old hardware and the hope carried into launch — reflected the larger story of Hubble itself.

Again and again, the telescope had faced trouble. Again and again, people found a way to fix it.

And as Atlantis prepared for its final servicing flight to Hubble, the engineers behind the scenes waited with the same mixture of fear and faith that had defined the program for years — hoping that an aging replacement computer, carefully brought back to readiness, would help carry Hubble into a new era of discovery.
